A parallel line starting at B on the x axis is labelled front of rod. A dashed x-bar axis from A (extending a little into the lower left) meets the front world line at C.
figures.what_it_teaches: Length is the distance between end events simultaneous for the measurer; the two observers pick different front-end events (B versus C), which is the whole origin of contraction.

redesign.idea: Rod-measurement lab: the world strip of a moving rod with two measuring crews, one per frame, each stamping the front end at their own 'now'.
redesign.interaction: Velocity and rest-length sliders; the learner clicks 'measure in O' or 'measure in O-bar' to highlight the chosen event pairs (AB or AC) and see numerical lengths l sqrt(1-v^2) and l; a train-in-tunnel animation plays alongside.

figures.label: Figure 1.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: Mutual time dilation: AB is the moving clock's elapsed time, AC is the elapsed time on O's clocks.
figures.visual_description: t and x axes with A at the origin and F on the x axis. A tilted t-bar line passes from A through B. A vertical dashed line rises through F and B (O's second clock). A horizontal dashed line joins C on the t axis to B. A hyperbola arc starts at D on the t axis and rises to B. A slanted dashed line from E on the t axis to B is O-bar's line of simultaneity, tangent to the hyperbola at B. On the t axis the points appear in the order A, E, D, C going up.
figures.what_it_teaches: O compares AB with AC (moving clock slow by 1/sqrt(1-v^2)); O-bar compares AB with AE and finds O's clock slow by the same factor; both use two clocks of their own and disagree only about simultaneity.
concepts: hyperbola tangent as line of simultaneity

redesign.idea: Who-is-slow referee: a split view of the same events with clock faces at A, B, C, D, E, F; the learner chooses which observer's simultaneity to adopt and sees which clock readings get compared.
redesign.interaction: Velocity slider; toggle 'O's simultaneity' (horizontal line through B) versus 'O-bar's simultaneity' (tilted line through B); clock faces display t_C = 1/sqrt(1-v^2), t_D = 1, t_E = sqrt(1-v^2); a scoreboard shows the ratio each observer computes, always the same factor.

figures.label: Figure 1.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: Twin paradox drawn in the stay-at-home twin's frame.
figures.visual_description: Vertical axis labelled Artemis' time axis, ticks at 25 yr and 50 yr; horizontal axis labelled Artemis' line of simultaneity. Diana's world line is a solid V opening to the left: it leaves the departure event P at the origin, reaches the reversal B at the 25 yr level (annotated as the moment Diana changes reference frames), and returns to the reunion dot at 50 yr. Each solid leg is flanked by two dashed lines: just outside it, a parallel dashed line labelled Diana's first (second) time-axis; just inside it, a dashed line through B labelled Diana's first (second) line of simultaneity, almost parallel to the leg because v = 0.96 makes the simultaneity slope 0.96 nearly equal to the world-line slope 1/0.96. The first dashed line meets Artemis' axis at A, just above P (about 2 yr); the second meets it at C, just below the reunion (about 48 yr).
figures.what_it_teaches: Diana's simultaneity line through B pivots when she changes frame, jumping from A (near the start of Artemis' history) to C (near its end); the nearly 46 years between A and C are the Earth time neither of her 'now' lines ever sweeps.

redesign.idea: Twin-trip simulator with simultaneity sweep: Diana's world line plus her current 'now' line sweeping across Artemis's world line, with both twins' age counters.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for speed and one-way proper duration; play the trip and watch the now-line hit Artemis's axis; at the turnaround the line swings and a highlighted segment of Artemis's life is skipped; age counters end at 14 and 50 years for the default 0.96c, 7 yr; an option adds a finite acceleration phase to show the swing smears out but the total is unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 1.16(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Diana's two simultaneity lines through the turnaround are both labelled with her time of 7 years.
figures.visual_description: Simplified version of Figure 1.15: axes with A at bottom and C at top of the vertical axis and B to the right; solid legs A-B and B-C; two dashed lines drawn just inside the legs, from B toward A and from B toward C. An annotation says Diana assigns t = 7 yr to both dashed lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: Diana's piecewise coordinates give the same time label to two widely separated sets of Earth events and never label the triangle ABC between them: a coverage gap, not a contradiction.

redesign.idea: Coordinate-coverage painter: the outgoing frame's region t-bar < 7 yr and the incoming frame's region after 7 yr are shaded in different colours, leaving the uncovered triangle blank.
redesign.interaction: Toggle which data the graduate students are told to record; expanding the outgoing frame's cutoff up to about 171 yr fills the triangle and reconciles the Earth-clock logs.

figures.label: Figure 1.16(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Euclidean analogy: switching to rotated axes midway while measuring a curve.
figures.visual_description: x and y axes plus a second pair x-bar and y-bar rotated counterclockwise by angle theta. A curve rises from A below the x axis through B and C to D. Several dashed lines parallel to the x-bar axis cross the curve, one passing through C.
figures.what_it_teaches: If you restart a measurement in rotated coordinates at the point with the same numerical coordinate value rather than at the same point, you skip part of the curve; Diana made the same mistake with time.

redesign.idea: Rotating-ruler analogy game: the learner measures arc length along a curve, is forced to switch to rotated axes at B, and must choose where to resume.
redesign.interaction: Drag the rotation angle; choose to resume at 'same point' or 'same y value'; the measured length and the missing section are displayed, then a button maps the same game onto Diana's spacetime diagram.

worked_examples.problem: Check that all three of Newton's laws keep their form when velocities are shifted by a constant V.
worked_examples.method: Substitute v' = v - V into each law: a constant velocity stays constant; differentiate to show a' = a; require force and mass to be the same for both observers so F = ma and action-reaction survive.
worked_examples.key_insight: Newtonian mechanics already obeys the principle of relativity because its dynamics depends on acceleration, not velocity; invariance requires specifying which quantities are frame-independent.
worked_examples.result: All three laws hold for both observers if F and m are invariant.
concepts: invariance of physical laws under a change of observer

worked_examples.problem: Express 10 joules in c = 1 units using only kilograms and meters (Exercise 1.1(a), worked in the text).
worked_examples.method: Write J = kg m^2 s^-2, substitute 1 s = 3e8 m so s^-2 = (9e16)^-1 m^-2; alternatively multiply by 1 = (3e8)^-2 s^2 m^-2 as many times as needed to cancel seconds.
worked_examples.key_insight: Treat c as a conversion factor equal to one; energy acquires units of mass, anticipating E = mc^2.

worked_examples.problem: Locate the space axis of an observer moving at v on the rest observer's spacetime diagram.
worked_examples.method: In the mover's frame, characterize its space axis by symmetric light echoes (emit at -a, receive at +a). In the rest frame mark E and R equally far from the origin along the tilted time axis, draw 45-degree rays from E forward and into R backward, and find their intersection P; join P to the origin.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the light postulate is needed, and the construction does not require knowing the time-axis calibration; the result is a tilted x-bar axis with slope v, the geometric heart of relativity of simultaneity.
worked_examples.result: x-bar axis is the line t = vx, tilted from the x axis by arctan|v|.

worked_examples.problem: Prove that the interval between two events is the same in all inertial frames.
worked_examples.method: Assume a linear map with coincident origins so the barred interval is a symmetric quadratic form in unbarred increments; impose vanishing on the light cone for all spatial directions to force M_{0i} = 0 and M_{ij} = -M_{00} delta_{ij}; conclude proportionality with factor phi(v). Use a transverse rod, whose end events are simultaneous in both frames by a light-echo argument, plus isotropy to get phi(|v|). Compose boosts v and -v to get phi^2 = 1 and choose the positive root from positivity of squared lengths.
worked_examples.key_insight: A symmetric structural argument (same null cone, isotropy, reversibility) pins the geometry without ever writing the Lorentz transformation.
worked_examples.result: Delta s-bar^2 = Delta s^2 (Eq. 1.7); corollaries: transverse lengths and transverse simultaneity agree.
concepts: proportionality of quadratic forms sharing a light cone

worked_examples.problem: Put unit scales on the moving observer's time and space axes.
worked_examples.method: Draw the hyperbola -t^2 + x^2 = -1 and note it is -t-bar^2 + x-bar^2 = -1 too; its crossing with the t axis is t = 1 and with the t-bar axis is t-bar = 1. Repeat with -t^2 + x^2 = 4 for the space axes.
worked_examples.key_insight: Invariant curves act as universal rulers; the Euclidean page distance of a tick is irrelevant.
worked_examples.result: Event B at t-bar = 1 has rest coordinates t = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2), x = v/sqrt(1 - v^2).

worked_examples.problem: Show that the tangent to a timelike hyperbola at any event is a line of simultaneity for the frame whose time axis passes through that event.
worked_examples.method: Observe the property at the vertex (tangent is t = const); redraw the picture in a boosted frame, which moves the vertex to any other point of the invariant hyperbola while preserving tangency.
worked_examples.key_insight: Symmetry transfers a trivial fact at one point to every point; this lemma later decides simultaneity in the reciprocity argument.
worked_examples.result: Tangent slope equals the frame velocity v.
concepts: hyperbola tangent as line of simultaneity

worked_examples.problem: Derive time dilation and interpret the interval as proper time.
worked_examples.method: Read event B from the calibrated diagram; then compute the interval in the clock's rest frame (Delta s^2 = -Delta t-bar^2) and in O (Delta t^2 - Delta x^2 with Delta x = v Delta t) and equate.
worked_examples.key_insight: The interval between events on a uniformly moving clock is literally what that clock reads; dilation compares one moving clock against two separated rest clocks.
worked_examples.result: Delta tau = Delta t sqrt(1 - v^2).

worked_examples.problem: Find the length in O of a rod of rest length l moving along x at speed v.
worked_examples.method: Take the rear on the t-bar axis; the front event C simultaneous (for the rod) with the rear at the origin has t-bar = 0, x-bar = l, so x_C = l/sqrt(1 - v^2) and t_C = v l/sqrt(1 - v^2) on the line t = vx. Follow the front's world line (slope v) back to t = 0: x_B = x_C - v t_C.
worked_examples.key_insight: Each observer's length is the proper distance between end events simultaneous in that observer's frame; choosing different events is the entire effect.

worked_examples.problem: Show without contradiction that each observer finds the other's clocks slow.
worked_examples.method: On Figure 1.14 list clock readings: O's origin clock and the moving clock agree at A; at B the moving clock reads 1 and O's clock at F reads 1/sqrt(1 - v^2). For the mover, the simultaneity line through B (tangent to the hyperbola) meets O's origin clock at E, where setting t-bar = (t - vx)/sqrt(1 - v^2) = 1 with x = 0 gives t = sqrt(1 - v^2). Compare ratios.
worked_examples.key_insight: The two observers perform different experiments using different simultaneity lines; they agree on every interval and every coincidence.
worked_examples.result: Both find the other's clocks slow by sqrt(1 - v^2).
concepts: hyperbola tangent as line of simultaneity

worked_examples.problem: Derive the Lorentz boost along x from the geometric results.
worked_examples.method: Start from the general linear map; impose the moving axis equations to get t-bar = alpha(t - vx), x-bar = sigma(x - vt); use the light ray linking (0, a) and (a, 0) in barred coordinates to set alpha = sigma; impose interval invariance to find alpha^2 = 1/(1 - v^2) and pick the positive root.
worked_examples.key_insight: The algebra is a transcription of the pictures: axis directions give ratios, light echoes give symmetry, invariance gives normalization.

worked_examples.problem: Combine a velocity W measured in a moving frame with the frame's velocity v.
worked_examples.method: Invert Eq. 1.12 for increments, form Delta x/Delta t, divide numerator and denominator by Delta t-bar; test W' = 1, W = 1, and small speeds.
worked_examples.key_insight: Relativistic composition cannot cross light speed and preserves it exactly; Galilean addition is its first-order limit.

worked_examples.problem: Twin paradox: Diana travels at 0.96c for 7 years of her time, turns around instantly, and returns; how old is each twin at reunion, and what do Diana's frame-by-frame records show?
worked_examples.method: With sqrt(1 - v^2) = 7/25, each 7-year leg lasts 25 years for Artemis, so 50 versus 14 years. In the outgoing frame, the Earth event simultaneous with the turnaround is at 7 x 7/25 = 1.96 yr; in the incoming frame it is at 50 - 1.96 = 48.04 yr. The outgoing frame's clocks would read 25/7 x 48.04 = about 171 yr at the later event. Reinterpret as Diana's coordinates omitting the triangle ABC.
worked_examples.key_insight: The asymmetry lies in Diana's change of inertial frame, which swings her simultaneity; stitched coordinates that skip part of spacetime produce the illusion of a paradox.
worked_examples.result: Artemis ages 50 years, Diana 14; logs show about 2 yr and 48 yr at Diana's 7 yr.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Soup in the dining car of a smoothly running train
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: absoluteness of acceleration in Newtonian mechanics
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Level soup at constant velocity gives no clue to speed, but soup climbing the bowl reveals the size and direction of any acceleration, singling out unaccelerated observers.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real trains vibrate; and the same soup test fails to detect gravitational acceleration, which is precisely the point made next.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle a train between cruising, braking and turning with a bowl whose surface tilts accordingly; a speedometer is hidden to emphasize that only changes register.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Soup held by an astronaut in orbit
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The orbiting astronaut's soup does not climb the bowl although the craft is continually accelerated by gravity, and astronauts in different orbits accelerate relative to each other while feeling nothing; gravity is unlike other forces.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Presented only as a puzzle; the equivalence principle that resolves it is postponed to Chapter 5.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side scenes: accelerating rocket with sloshing soup versus orbiting capsule with calm soup, plus two capsules in different orbits whose separation changes.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lattice of rigid rods with a clock at every intersection, synchronized by a GPS-like system
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Makes the abstract coordinate system tangible: every event has a nearby clock to timestamp it on the spot, removing signal delays from the definition of measurement.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rigid rods are an idealization that conflicts with finite signal speeds under acceleration; GPS itself requires relativistic (including gravitational) corrections.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Zoomable 3D lattice where clicking an event lights the nearest clock and records coordinates, contrasted with a single eye at the origin receiving delayed light.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Light-year as a unit of distance (footnote 4)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Readers already accept measuring distance by light-travel time; measuring time in meters is the same idea turned around.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Light-years hide c inside a named unit rather than setting it to 1.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Changing rotated coordinates partway through measuring a curve's length
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: If after switching to rotated axes you resume from the point with the old coordinate value instead of the old point, part of the curve is skipped; Diana does the same with her time coordinate at the turnaround.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Euclidean rotations preserve positive-definite distance, while boosts preserve an indefinite interval, so the skipped piece corresponds to a region of spacetime rather than a segment of one curve.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Interactive curve-measuring game with a forced axis rotation and a choice of where to resume, then morph the same game into Minkowski geometry.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Graduate students riding every clock and filing dispatches to a computer room
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Turns the observer's data-gathering network into people who log Earth's clock reading at the moment they pass it, making clear that an observation is local and that conclusions depend on which reports you collect.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Humorous; the image of people riding clocks may distract from the point that the records are simply coordinates.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Animated fleet of clock-riders passing Earth, each dropping a timestamped report into a database that the learner queries by Diana-time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Invariant hyperbolae as the spacetime analogue of circles (Exercise 1.19)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Rotations preserve x^2 + y^2 and move points along circles; boosts preserve -t^2 + x^2 and move points along hyperbolae, with rapidity playing the role of angle.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The analogy breaks at the light cone, where hyperbolae degenerate and rapidity is unbounded, and 'angles' between timelike and spacelike directions are not ordinary angles.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Dual panel: a rotation slider moves points on circles, a rapidity slider moves points on hyperbolae; matching tables of cos/sin and cosh/sinh.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Clock comparisons as experiments with two clocks versus one
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames each rate comparison as an experiment requiring two synchronized local clocks to time one moving clock, like timing a runner with two stopwatches at start and finish; different observers use different stopwatch pairs.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The stopwatch image is implicit; the text does not use sports language.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Race-timing mini-game where each frame's officials place stopwatches and see their verdicts diverge only because of synchronization.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: What an observer 'sees' (light arriving at the eye) defines when events happen.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: An inertial observer assigns each event the reading of the clock located at that event; visual arrival times mix in signal delays and give a different, non-standard notion of simultaneity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday seeing feels instantaneous, and popular language says observers 'see' clocks slow.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Time dilation and length contraction are optical illusions caused by the finite travel time of signals.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They remain after all signal delays are corrected; they stem from observers' different, equally reasonable definitions of 'now'.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Delays are real and familiar (thunder after lightning), so they look like a natural explanation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If each observer finds the other's clocks slow, the theory contradicts itself or violates the principle of relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The two observers perform different comparisons with different pairs of their own synchronized clocks; they agree on all intervals and disagree only on simultaneity, so mutual slowing is exactly what relativity requires.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Galilean thinking assumes a single universal comparison of rates.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Special relativity really does contain paradoxes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The classic paradoxes are ill-posed problems that sneak in Galilean assumptions; SR is internally consistent and extensively tested.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbooks and popular accounts present them as paradoxes, and careless resolutions leave doubt.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Time dilation depends on how a clock is built, so some clocks (or living things) might be exempt.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Dilation follows from spacetime geometry and applies to every process at rest in the moving frame, from atomic clocks to heartbeats and particle decays.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Mechanical intuitions about moving machinery suggest motion could disturb particular mechanisms.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A point that is farther from the origin on the spacetime diagram is separated by a larger interval.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The page's Euclidean distance is irrelevant; the unit tick on a moving time axis looks farther out yet lies on the same invariant hyperbola as the rest tick.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Diagrams are drawn on Euclidean paper, and we read distances off pictures automatically.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The moving observer's space axis is the same horizontal line as the rest observer's; only the time axis tilts.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Keeping light at 45 degrees forces the moving space axis to tilt by the same angle toward the light line, so the frames disagree on simultaneity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Galilean relativity only the time axis tilts, and absolute simultaneity feels obvious.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: General relativity is needed whenever an observer accelerates, while special relativity only handles inertial observers.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The essential difference is gravity: SR can analyse accelerated motion (as in the twin appendix), but it cannot describe gravitational fields; GR's name reflects a secondary feature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The names 'special' and 'general' suggest a split by type of observer.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The notation Delta s^2 means the change in some quantity s^2.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It always denotes the square of Delta s (and is allowed to be negative); some authors call it the squared interval.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Standard calculus notation would read Delta applied to s^2.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: There is a single universal 'now' dividing all of spacetime into past and future.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In SR an event's present is only the event itself; between its absolute past and absolute future lies an elsewhere whose time order relative to the event depends on the frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The Galilean picture matches everyday experience at low speeds.
concepts: causal structure (absolute past, future and elsewhere)

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The twin paradox is resolved by the forces the travelling twin feels during acceleration, which somehow slow her clock.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book's resolution uses no dynamics: Diana's switch between inertial frames changes which Earth events she calls simultaneous, and her naive stitching of coordinates leaves a region unrecorded; ages follow from proper time along each world line.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Acceleration is the obvious physical asymmetry, and many popular accounts stop there.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An object falling into a black hole never reaches the horizon because exterior coordinate time to get there is infinite.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Infinite coordinate time reflects coordinates that do not cover the interior; the object crosses in finite proper time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate time is easily mistaken for physical time, as Diana did.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Moving objects shrink in every direction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only lengths along the relative velocity contract; perpendicular lengths are identical in both frames, as shown within the interval invariance proof.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The phrase 'moving objects shrink' is often stated without direction.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Velocities simply add, so two speeds below c can combine to exceed c.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Relativistic composition (W + v)/(1 + Wv) never reaches 1 from sub-light inputs and keeps light at 1.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Galilean addition works in every everyday situation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because frames disagree about time and length, there is nothing objective in relativity ('everything is relative').
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The interval, the light-cone causal order and coincidences of events are shared by all observers; only coordinate-dependent descriptions differ.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name 'relativity' and the emphasis on disagreements invite this reading.

thought_experiments.name: Light echo defines the moving frame's 'now'
thought_experiments.setup: A moving observer sends a pulse from its origin at time -a toward a mirror and receives the echo at +a; the reflection event is transcribed into the rest frame.
thought_experiments.lesson: Simultaneity is defined operationally by light and differs between frames.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Build-the-axis interactive in which the learner fires pulses and watches the reflection events line up along a tilted line.

thought_experiments.name: Transverse rod pinged from a passing clock
thought_experiments.setup: A rod lies along y at rest in O; a clock of the moving frame passes midway between its ends and sends light to both ends, receiving both echoes at one event.
thought_experiments.lesson: End events of a transverse rod are simultaneous in both frames, so its length and the factor phi depend only on speed.
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D scene with expanding light spheres from the moving clock reaching both rod ends.

thought_experiments.name: There and back again: boosting by v and then by -v
thought_experiments.setup: Frame O-bar moves at v relative to O; a third frame moves at -v relative to O-bar and is therefore O itself.
thought_experiments.lesson: Applying the proportionality twice must give the identity, so phi^2 = 1 and the interval is invariant.

thought_experiments.name: Two observers each timing the other's clock
thought_experiments.setup: Clocks of O and O-bar coincide at A; later O's second clock meets O-bar's clock at B, while O-bar compares with O's first clock at the event it considers simultaneous with B.
thought_experiments.lesson: Mutual slowing is consistent because each uses two synchronized clocks of its own and disagrees about the other's synchronization.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Who-is-slow referee widget with toggled simultaneity lines.

thought_experiments.name: Diana and Artemis with graduate students riding clocks
thought_experiments.setup: Diana flies at 0.96c for 7 years and back; in each leg her frame's clocks are staffed by students logging Earth's clock whenever they pass it.
thought_experiments.lesson: Earth-clock logs at the same Diana-time differ wildly (about 2 vs 48 years) because they record different Earth events; coordinates stitched from two frames omit a spacetime triangle.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Twin-trip simulator with a database of student dispatches the learner can query.

thought_experiments.name: Soup on the train and soup in orbit
thought_experiments.setup: A diner on a smooth train watches soup under constant velocity and acceleration; an astronaut in orbit holds soup despite being accelerated by gravity.
thought_experiments.lesson: Acceleration is detectable except when it is gravitational, which is why gravity does not fit SR.
concepts: absoluteness of acceleration in Newtonian mechanics
thought_experiments.app_idea: Paired animation of sloshing versus calm soup in accelerating and freely falling vehicles.

thought_experiments.name: Pole in the barn (Exercise 1.17)
thought_experiments.setup: A 20 m pole carried at 0.8c toward a 15 m barn whose door is shut once the pole is inside; the pole's front hits the far wall.
thought_experiments.lesson: Whether the pole is 'inside' at one moment depends on simultaneity; the door-closing and wall-hitting events can be ordered differently in different frames when they are spacelike separated, and rigid stopping is impossible.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Barn-and-pole spacetime diagram with draggable frame velocity and event markers for door and wall.

historical_notes.event: Proposed that bodies in uniform motion stay so unless acted on and that uniform motion cannot be detected.
historical_notes.significance: Origin of the principle of relativity, the first postulate of SR.

historical_notes.event: Argued in the Principia that acceleration, unlike velocity, is absolute and detectable (cited via Williams 1968).
Published special relativity, adding the universality of light speed.
historical_notes.significance: Overturned Galilean velocity addition and absolute simultaneity.

historical_notes.event: Recast SR as the geometry of a four-dimensional spacetime.
historical_notes.significance: Launched the geometric viewpoint that led Einstein to general relativity and that this book adopts.

historical_notes.event: Completed general relativity, extending SR to include gravitation.
historical_notes.significance: Marks the destination toward which the chapter's geometric approach points.

historical_notes.event: Interferometer experiment finding no effect of Earth's motion on light speed.
historical_notes.significance: Earliest direct evidence for the second postulate, though its influence on Einstein is uncertain.

historical_notes.event: Discovery of a coordinate system covering both the inside and outside of a black hole.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates how coordinate systems can fail to cover spacetime. Historically, Synge (1950) and Kruskal (mid-1950s, published 1960 alongside Szekeres) found complete coverings, and Finkelstein (1958) gave coordinates regular across the horizon, so the book's date is reasonable.

historical_notes.event: Guided the science of the film Interstellar, which dramatizes gravitational time dilation near a black hole, and later shared the 2017 Nobel Prize for the first gravitational-wave detection.
historical_notes.significance: Connects the twin effect to gravity and to the book's later observational chapters.

applications_and_observations.topic: Particle accelerators as tests of SR
applications_and_observations.details: Accelerators routinely drive particles to nearly light speed, repeatedly confirming SR predictions; the book calls SR perhaps the best-tested law of physics.
Early evidence that light speed does not depend on the observer's motion.
Offered as the practical means of synchronizing the clocks of an idealized inertial lattice.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our note: GPS clocks need a net relativistic correction of about +38 microseconds per day (special and general), so GPS synchronization is itself relativistic.

applications_and_observations.details: A pion's rest half-life is lengthened in the lab when it moves at 0.999c, as required by the principle of relativity.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Rest half-life 2.5e-8 s; at v = 0.999, 1/sqrt(1 - v^2) is about 22.4, giving 5.6e-7 s.

applications_and_observations.details: Everyday SI quantities re-expressed with c = 1, e.g. energy as mass.

applications_and_observations.topic: Relativistic round trip of the twin appendix
applications_and_observations.details: Quantitative twin paradox at 24/25 of light speed.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: v = 0.96, sqrt(1 - v^2) = 0.28; Diana 7 yr each way (about 2.2e8 s), Artemis 25 yr each way; totals 14 vs 50 yr; Earth-clock logs about 1.96 yr and 48.04 yr; outgoing-frame date of the later Earth event about 171 yr.

applications_and_observations.details: Astronauts feel no acceleration even though gravity continually bends their paths, and astronauts in different orbits accelerate relative to each other; this is why gravity needs GR.
Exterior coordinates assign infinite coordinate time to reach the horizon although the infalling body crosses in finite proper time, because those coordinates do not cover the interior.
Each star sees the next receding at 0.9c; rapidities add, so the Nth star's speed approaches but never reaches 1.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Rapidity per step artanh(0.9) is about 1.47 (our computation).

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 with time measured in meters (1 s = 3 x 10^8 m). Consequences: energy and momentum carry units of kg, acceleration of 1/m, force of kg/m, and pressure and energy density of kg/m^3.
notation_and_conventions.notes: G is not set to 1 in this chapter.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Time enters the interval with a minus sign and the three spatial terms with plus signs, signature (-+++); timelike intervals are therefore negative and equal minus the squared proper time.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Many authors use the opposite overall sign; check before comparing formulas.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Always means (Delta s)^2, never Delta(s^2); may be negative.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Footnote 7; some authors call it the squared interval and reserve 'interval' for sqrt|Delta s^2|.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Events are calligraphic capitals (A, B, P, ...); the calligraphic O is reserved for observers.
Time listed first: (t, x, y, z) = (x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3); superscripts are labels, so (x^3)^2 is z squared; {x^alpha} is the full set.
Greek indices (alpha, beta, mu, nu) run over 0-3; Latin indices (a, b, i, j, k, l) over 1-3.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Footnote 6: other books reverse or rename these; footnote 8: Greek letters used as coefficients (alpha, beta, gamma, sigma in §1.9) are not indices.

notation_and_conventions.convention: A second observer and its coordinates carry an overbar (or tilde; the print uses both for the same frame): O-bar, t-bar, x-bar. A third frame in the invariance proof and Diana's incoming frame carry a double overbar.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The export often garbles the bar/tilde/double bar distinctions; consult renders.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Sums are written with explicit summation signs in this chapter (e.g. Eq. 1.2); the summation convention is not yet in use.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Einstein summation is introduced in Chapter 2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The standard boost has the second frame moving at +v along x with parallel axes and coincident origins; transverse coordinates unchanged.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Rotated axes give more complicated formulas, rarely needed.

notation_and_conventions.convention: u defined by v = tanh u (Exercises 1.18-1.19); the term rapidity is not used.
No dedicated symbol; written out as 1/sqrt(1 - v^2). The letter gamma in §1.9 is an unrelated coefficient.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Contrast with most texts that write gamma for the Lorentz factor.

margin_notes.summary: Footnote 1: Einstein's paper dates from 1905 and Minkowski's spacetime lecture from 1908; English translations are collected in the Dover volume The Principle of Relativity.
Footnote 2: a wry remark that physicists like idealizations, attached to the perfectly smooth track.
Footnote 3: points to an excerpt of Newton's Principia discussion of absolute acceleration in Williams (1968).
Footnote 4 (missing from the export, recovered from the page render): compares time-in-meters with the familiar light-year, a distance defined by light-travel time.

Footnote 5 (missing from the export, recovered from the page render): 'space' for spacetime means a continuum of points without assuming meaningful Euclidean distances; this is a first example of a manifold, defined in Chapter 5.
Footnote 6: Greek/Latin index conventions are not universal; always check a source's usage.
Footnote 7: terminology for the interval varies (some say squared interval), proper time and distance are defined universally, and Delta s^2 means (Delta s)^2.
Footnote 8 (missing from the export, recovered from the page render): not every Greek letter denotes an index; alpha, beta, gamma, sigma in the boost are ordinary coefficients.
Aside in §1.1: the author wishes earlier physicists had chosen better names than 'special' and 'general' relativity.
Aside in §1.12: the film Interstellar dramatizes the twin effect via black-hole gravity; Kip Thorne guided it and later shared the Nobel Prize for gravitational-wave detection.

notable.summary: A long checklist of constructions on one diagram: world lines, a boosted frame at v = 0.5, hyperbolae of interval +1, -1 and 0, calibration ticks, lines of constant t and constant t-bar, and a photon bounced between a moving mirror and a fixed detector.
notable.why_notable: Turns the chapter's geometric method into a hands-on drawing drill; ideal template for an interactive construction tutorial.

notable.summary: An experimenter sends particle bursts to two symmetric detectors which return signals that meet at the origin; the reader verifies simultaneity in the lab frame, then redraws it for an observer moving at 0.75 and decides which detector fired first, and computes the interval both ways.
notable.why_notable: A concrete lab-style version of the light-echo simultaneity argument using slower-than-light signals.

notable.summary: Completes the invariance proof: derive the light-cone form of the quadratic expression, use sign reversal of spatial increments to kill the mixed terms, and use arbitrary directions to force isotropy.
notable.why_notable: Fills the step the text calls easy; needed for anyone who wants the proof airtight.

notable.summary: Uses the tangent property on Figure 1.14 to show the moving observer sees O's clock lag, via a relation between squared intervals.
notable.why_notable: Printed part (b) names AC but the stated factor (1 - v^2) holds for AE; for AC the factor is 1/(1 - v^2). Worth flagging to learners.

notable.summary: Near-light-speed approximations for dilation, contraction and velocity addition with |v| = 1 - epsilon, plus error estimates.
notable.why_notable: Printed part (b) appears to invert the contraction factor relative to Exercise 1.14(b); a good catch-the-error exercise.

notable.summary: The pole-and-barn problem at 0.8c with a 20 m pole and 15 m barn: lengths in each frame, timing and interval between door closing and wall impact, and what 'inside' means, finishing with a spacetime diagram.
notable.why_notable: The classic paradox named in §1.11 turned into a multi-part investigation; excellent for a guided tutor dialogue.

notable.summary: Shows collinear velocities compose by adding velocity parameters (v = tanh u) and applies it to a chain of stars each receding at 0.9c from the previous one, asking for an exact and a large-N answer.
notable.why_notable: Introduces rapidity, which is not in the main text, and makes the light-speed ceiling vivid.

notable.summary: Rewrites the boost with hyperbolic functions, proves interval invariance from cosh^2 - sinh^2 = 1, and asks for parallels with Euclidean rotations.
notable.why_notable: Makes explicit the rotation analogy used in the twin appendix.

notable.summary: Show that timelike-separated events occur at the same place in some frame and spacelike-separated events at the same time in some frame.
notable.why_notable: Gives the operational meaning of proper time and proper distance.

difficulty.notes: Algebra never goes beyond quadratic forms and square roots, but the chapter asks readers to abandon Euclidean readings of diagrams and absolute simultaneity, and the invariance proof and reciprocity discussion require careful attention to which events are compared. It assumes prior exposure to algebraic SR, so a true beginner may need a warm-up. The export mangles bar/tilde/double-bar frame labels and drops three footnotes; a few printed slips (Eq. 1.8 frame subscript, Exercises 1.12(b) and 1.15(b)) can confuse careful readers.

Kip Thorne's Nobel Prize for gravitational-wave detection, mentioned in the bibliography, links to the later chapter on gravitational radiation.
Readable, more detailed introduction that guided the chapter's treatment; freely available online.

teaching_gems.gem: Build the moving frame's space axis from a single light-echo experiment before any formula exists.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see relativity of simultaneity forced on them by the light postulate alone, so it feels inevitable rather than decreed.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-by-step construction widget: place emission and reception on the tilted time axis, draw 45-degree rays, click the intersection; contrast with a Galilean mode where the echo fails to close.

teaching_gems.gem: Prove interval invariance by structure (same light cone implies proportional quadratic forms; isotropy; there-and-back boost) rather than by plugging into the Lorentz transformation.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows why invariance must hold, avoids circularity, and previews the style of reasoning (symmetry plus linear algebra) that GR relies on.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Proof navigator: each of the three stages is a card with a small interactive check (e.g. the rod echo in 3D, a composition of boost sliders returning to identity).

teaching_gems.gem: Use invariant hyperbolae as rulers to calibrate every frame's axes, pointing out that the moving tick looks farther away but is not.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Directly confronts the Euclidean-paper intuition that sabotages diagram reading, and gives a reusable graphical tool.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Calibration drag game with a Euclidean ruler that disagrees with the interval readout.

teaching_gems.gem: Wherever a timelike hyperbola is touched by a straight line, that line is the 'now' line of the observer whose world line runs from the origin to the touching point.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A symmetric argument turns a trivial fact at the vertex into a universal lemma that later decides who is slow in mutual dilation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Slide a point along a hyperbola; the time axis and tangent follow, slopes displayed as 1/v and v.

teaching_gems.gem: Count clocks: a rate comparison uses two synchronized clocks of one frame against one clock of the other, so the two observers are doing different experiments.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces a vague 'it depends on the frame' with a concrete accounting of which events are compared, dissolving the reciprocity worry.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Referee widget with clock faces at A, B, C, D, E, F and toggleable simultaneity lines showing each observer's comparison and identical slowdown ratio.

teaching_gems.gem: Proper time is what a clock physically reads between two events it passes through; the interval is therefore measurable, not merely a formula.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Grounds the central invariant in an operation learners can imagine, preparing for proper time along curved world lines and the metric in GR.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Clock-along-world-line tool: pick two timelike events, a clock travels straight between them and its reading matches sqrt(-Delta s^2) in every frame.

teaching_gems.gem: Dissect the twin paradox as a coordinate-coverage failure: Diana's two frames' records skip a triangle of spacetime, illustrated by a Euclidean rotation analogy.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Moves the explanation from vague 'acceleration' talk to a precise, generalizable lesson about coordinates that pays off at black-hole horizons.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Coverage painter over the twin diagram plus a rotated-axes curve-measuring game that morphs into the spacetime version.

teaching_gems.gem: Measure time in meters so that c = 1 is a statement about units, then treat c as a conversion factor one can multiply by freely.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Removes a large number from every formula and makes light lines diagonal, while the conversion-factor view keeps SI results recoverable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Unit converter that animates inserting factors of c to cancel seconds, e.g. turning joules into kilograms.

teaching_gems.gem: Contrast the Galilean universal 'now' with the relativistic light-cone partition and show that two events have different but overlapping pasts and futures.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One picture replaces the absolute-time worldview with an invariant causal structure that learners can reason with.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Signal-speed morph slider from infinite to c that folds the 'now' line into cones, with draggable events showing common past and future.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Linearity of the coordinate transformation is simply assumed in the invariance proof, without appeal to homogeneity of spacetime or the principle of inertia.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful learners may feel the proof is circular or incomplete.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short argument: uniform motion must map to uniform motion and no event is special, which forces an affine map; set origins to coincide.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Key algebra is deferred with phrases such as 'easy to show' (Eq. 1.4 via Exercise 1.8), 'can easily be shown' (alpha = sigma) and 'straightforward algebra' (alpha).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Novices may not see how the light-cone condition kills cross terms or how alpha = sigma follows.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide expandable worked steps or have the tutor walk through the sign-flip trick and the light-ray condition explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The argument that phi depends only on |v| is terse: it relies on the rod's squared lengths being related by phi and on isotropy, but does not spell out why the ratio cannot depend on direction.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The logic of stage one of the proof can feel like hand-waving.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present it as: reversing the direction of v while keeping the transverse rod fixed is a spatial reflection that cannot change the rod's length, so phi(v) = phi(-v) and, by rotation, phi depends only on speed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Figure 1.7's perspective drawing is hard to read, and the requirement that the clock pass midway between the rod ends is left implicit (Exercise 1.9 asks for it).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot see why both echoes return together.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use an orbitable 3D visualization with explicit light cones from P and a top-down view of the x-y plane.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed Eq. 1.8 labels the numerator 'measured in O' although Delta t-bar is measured by the moving observer's clock (confirmed on the page render).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses which observer's measurement sits on each side of the dilation formula.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the numerator as the proper time of the clock at rest in O-bar.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 1.12(b) asserts (Delta s^2)_AC = (1 - v^2)(Delta s^2)_AB, but with C at t = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2) the factor for AC is 1/(1 - v^2); the stated factor applies to AE.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students checking the calculation will get a contradiction and doubt their understanding.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Read AE in place of AC, or keep AC and invert the factor; flag in tutor materials.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 1.15(b) as printed gives Delta x approx Delta x-bar / sqrt(2 epsilon), inconsistent with Exercise 1.14(b), where the contraction factor multiplies; the near-light limit should be sqrt(2 epsilon) times Delta x-bar.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conclude that lengths grow near light speed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct to Delta x approx sqrt(2 epsilon) Delta x-bar, and state clearly which length is proper.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In Figure 1.15 the labels A and C sit very close to the departure and reunion dots, because at v = 0.96 Diana's simultaneity lines almost hug her world line; Figure 1.16(a) also writes an unbarred t = 7 yr for what is Diana's own time coordinate.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may take A as the departure and C as the reunion, and then cannot see why the text calls them simultaneous with B or where the 2 yr, 48 yr and 171 yr figures come from.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Redraw at a lower speed (e.g. v = 0.6) or mark A and C with their Artemis times (1.96 yr, 48.04 yr) and use a barred time label for Diana.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The same moving frame is written with both tilde and overbar in nearby passages, and the double bar for a third frame is easy to lose (the export garbles these systematically).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers cannot tell whether two or three frames are in play in the invariance proof and the twin appendix.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Adopt distinct names or colours for each frame in app materials.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The appendix dates the first coordinates covering both inside and outside a black hole to the mid-1950s without names.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor: learners who look it up will find several candidates and dates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: If asked, mention Synge (1950) and Kruskal (worked out mid-1950s, published 1960, simultaneously with Szekeres), with Finkelstein (1958) giving coordinates regular across the horizon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Proper time is treated only for straight world lines; the twin's total age is obtained by adding two straight legs with an instantaneous turn, and the statement that accelerated observers cannot keep synchronized clocks is not demonstrated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think SR cannot handle continuous acceleration or proper time along curves.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Preview proper time as the integral of sqrt(1 - v^2) dt along any world line and show a smooth-turnaround version giving nearly the same result.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that nothing moves faster than light is used when interpreting light cones before it has been argued.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may wonder whether causality is assumed or derived.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point ahead to the velocity-addition closure and to later energy arguments; note that tachyons would break causal ordering of elsewhere events.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Velocity addition is treated only for collinear motion; transverse velocities, aberration and the Doppler effect are absent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners lack tools for non-collinear problems that appear in astrophysics.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Supplement with the general velocity transformation or defer to four-velocity methods in Chapter 2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chapter assumes prior algebraic SR (it names E = mc^2 and mass-energy conversion as known) and does not motivate the postulates experimentally beyond brief mentions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner with no SR background may find the pace fast and the motivation thin.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Offer an optional primer on muon/pion lifetimes and light-speed experiments before §1.4.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 1.7 names a transformation coefficient with the Greek letter nu, which is nearly indistinguishable in print from the italic v used for relative velocity, and writes the index range of M with a Latin b ('alpha, b = 0, ..., 3').
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers (and text exports) easily read the coefficient as the velocity itself, and the Latin b contradicts the stated index conventions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In adapted versions rename the coefficient (e.g. delta) and write the range as alpha, beta = 0, ..., 3.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Two firecrackers explode at opposite ends of a moving train. Who decides whether they went off at the same time?' Let the learner commit before introducing the light-echo construction.
Check early whether the learner distinguishes 'when I see it' from 'when it happened'; if not, spend time on the rod-and-clock lattice before any diagrams.

Order of explanation that mirrors the book: postulates -> observer as coordinate grid -> c = 1 units -> spacetime diagrams -> tilted axes via light echoes -> interval invariance -> light cones -> hyperbola calibration -> dilation and contraction -> reciprocity -> Lorentz transformation -> velocity addition -> twin paradox.
When drawing a boost, always draw the 45-degree light line first and have the learner place the moving axes symmetrically about it; ask 'why can't the moving x-axis stay horizontal?'
Check for understanding of invariance: give two events in one frame, have the learner compute Delta s^2, then boost and recompute; ask what changed and what didn't.
Common question: 'Which clock is really slow?' Answer by making the learner list the three clocks used in each observer's comparison and which events each observer calls simultaneous.
Common question: 'Is time dilation just because light takes time to reach you?' Emphasize that every observer corrects for delays; the effect is in the definition of simultaneity.
For Euclidean-intuition errors, point at the calibration tick on the moving time axis and ask the learner to compute its interval; the surprise that it equals -1 is instructive.
Use the hyperbola-tangent lemma as a tool: before revealing it, ask the learner to guess the moving frame's simultaneity line through a point on a hyperbola.

In the twin paradox, avoid leading with acceleration forces. Ask the learner to compute both twins' proper times first (14 vs 50 years at 0.96c for 7-year legs), then examine Diana's simultaneity lines before and after the turnaround.
Flag the printed slips when relevant: Eq. 1.8's subscript, Exercise 1.12(b) (AC should be AE) and Exercise 1.15(b) (factor should multiply). Learners who hit them should be reassured.

Adapt to level: for beginners, do everything on the t-x diagram with v = 0.6 (factor 1.25) and avoid the quadratic-form proof; for advanced learners, ask them to reproduce the three-stage invariance proof and connect it to the metric tensor.

Link forward: when learners ask why so much geometry, preview that in GR the interval becomes a position-dependent metric and light cones tilt near black holes, where coordinates can fail just as Diana's did.

Quick check questions: classify (0,0,0,0) and (-1,1,0,0); state which lengths do not contract; give the composite of 0.9 and 0.9; explain in one sentence why the elsewhere region has no invariant time order.
If the learner asks why units with c = 1 are legitimate, do a live conversion (10 J to kg) treating c as a factor of 1 to show nothing physical is lost.
